description: Registry of Sufyan Ahmad's teaching labs. Rendered by index.html (#lab teaser), labs.html (library) and lab.html?slug= (detail page), and used to keep every new project distinct from the existing ones.

projects.name: SLO-Driven Progressive Delivery with Automated Rollback
projects.summary: When a team releases a new version of an app, this system first gives it to only a few users and checks if it works well. If it does, more users get it step by step. If it doesn't, the system automatically switches everyone back to the old version.
projects.problem: Usually a new version goes to all users at once. If it has a bug, everyone is affected, and someone has to notice it and undo it by hand, often in the middle of the night.
projects.engineering_problem: Release safety: gate production rollouts on SLO/error-budget signals and roll back automatically.
projects.architecture: Argo Rollouts canary with background AnalysisTemplate querying Prometheus per pod-template hash; multi-window burn-rate alerts; Grafana provisioned as code; kind-based e2e in GitHub Actions.
projects.unique_capability: SLIs/SLOs, error budgets, multi-window multi-burn-rate alerting, progressive delivery with automated rollback, fail-safe analysis.
projects.tagline: New app versions are tested on a few users first and undone automatically if something breaks.
projects.benefit: Bad releases reach only a few users for less than a minute and are undone automatically, so teams can release often without fear, and nobody has to watch every release.
projects.simple_name: Safe app releases that undo themselves

projects.name: Automated Linux Server Hardening & Monitoring with Ansible
projects.simple_name: One command that locks down a new server
projects.summary: You run one command and a brand-new Linux server is made safe: only people with the right key can log in, unwanted connections are blocked, attackers who keep guessing passwords are blocked automatically, and security updates install by themselves. A dashboard then keeps watching every server.
projects.problem: A new server is quite open by default and bots start guessing passwords within minutes. Securing it by hand takes long, every server ends up a bit different, and nobody notices when someone later switches a protection off.
projects.benefit: Every server gets exactly the same protection in a few minutes, its security score is measured (61 → 77 in the lab), and running the same command again shows and fixes anything that was changed by hand.
projects.tagline: One command makes a new Linux server secure, and a dashboard keeps checking that it stays that way.
projects.engineering_problem: Configuration drift and inconsistent manual hardening of Linux servers.
projects.architecture: Nine idempotent Ansible roles with validate-before-write (sshd -t, nft -c, visudo) and lockout guards; Molecule on Ubuntu 24.04/Debian 12/Debian 13; Docker lab with real SSH, attacker and Prometheus/Grafana; check/diff drift detection; Lynis score exported via the node_exporter textfile collector.
projects.unique_capability: Safe, repeatable server hardening with measured before/after security scores, drift detection and monitoring of the protections themselves.

projects.name: PostgreSQL Backups You Can Trust: Restore Drills & Point-in-Time Recovery
projects.simple_name: Database backups that are tested every night
projects.summary: Every change in the database is copied to safe, encrypted storage within a minute. Every night the system practises a restore on a spare copy and checks that nothing is missing, like a fire drill. If someone deletes data by mistake, one command brings the database back to the second before it happened.
projects.problem: Many teams have backups but never try to restore them. On the day they really need them, they discover the backups are broken, too old, or that nobody knows the password, and the data is gone.
projects.benefit: You know every morning that the backups really work, how long a restore takes (6 seconds in the lab) and how much data could be lost (under a minute). An alert appears long before the backups are needed.
projects.tagline: Backups are restored and checked automatically every night, so you know they work before you need them.
projects.engineering_problem: Untested backups: unknown restorability, RTO and RPO; no point-in-time recovery.
projects.architecture: PostgreSQL 18 archives WAL through a dedicated pgBackRest repo host (mutual TLS) into encrypted S3; full/diff/incremental backups, daily verify and an automatic restore drill with amcheck; isolated networks; Pushgateway + Prometheus alerts; point-in-time and lost-volume recovery scripts.
projects.unique_capability: Proves restorability every day with measured RTO/RPO, and is tested against an accidental DROP TABLE, a lost database disk, a storage outage, bit rot and a lost encryption key.

projects.name: Zero-Trust Software Supply Chain for Kubernetes: Signed Builds, SBOMs & Admission Control
projects.simple_name: Only code we built ourselves can run in production
projects.summary: Every app our pipeline builds gets a digital seal and three signed papers: where it came from, a security scan, and a list of everything inside. A guard at the door of the cluster checks the seal and the papers before anything starts. No seal from our pipeline, no entry.
projects.problem: Most clusters run any app that sits in the company's image store. If an attacker steals that store's password, slips a bad step into the build, or changes one line in git, their code runs in production and nobody notices.
projects.benefit: A stolen password or a sneaky git change is no longer enough to run code in production. Each release is attacked automatically before it ships, and an alert appears when something is blocked or when an app already running turns out to have a serious security hole.
projects.tagline: Production only runs apps that carry our pipeline's seal, so a stolen password is not enough to get in.
projects.engineering_problem: Clusters trust registry contents and git, not proof of origin; CI pipelines themselves are attack paths.
projects.architecture: GitHub Actions builds a distroless Go image, gates on Trivy, pushes by digest and signs keylessly with cosign (OIDC, Fulcio, Rekor) plus SLSA provenance, vulnerability and SBOM attestations; an e2e attack test runs on a fresh kind cluster before the digest is promoted to git; Argo CD deploys; Kyverno CEL policies verify the release identity, provenance, scan and SBOM at admission; Trivy Operator and Prometheus watch what runs.
projects.unique_capability: Refuses images signed by a different workflow of the same repository (injected-workflow attacks), tampered and unsigned images, and malicious GitOps commits, and proves it on every release.

projects.name: EKS DevSecOps Platform: React on Amazon EKS with Terraform and GitHub Actions
projects.simple_name: A website on AWS Kubernetes, built safely, tested by attacking it
projects.summary: Code builds a private network and a Kubernetes cluster on AWS, and every code change is checked for security problems and put online automatically, without any stored cloud password. Then the setup was attacked on purpose, the two weak spots it found were fixed, and everything was deleted again.
projects.problem: Putting an app on Kubernetes is quick, but it is easy to leave cloud passwords in the build system, ship software with known security holes, expose servers to the internet, or forget a test cluster that keeps costing money.
projects.benefit: Updates go live in under four minutes with security checks on every step, no permanent cloud password exists that could leak, users saw no errors during updates after the fix, and the whole lab cost well under one dollar because it was cleaned up and checked.
projects.tagline: A secure path from code to the internet on AWS, proven by attacking it and cleaned up afterwards.
projects.engineering_problem: Long-lived CI cloud keys, unscanned images, exposed nodes, over-privileged pods, rollout errors and forgotten lab resources.
projects.architecture: Terraform builds a two-AZ VPC (private nodes, public ALB only, NAT, flow logs), EKS 1.37 with KMS-encrypted secrets, audit logs, access entries, IMDSv2 hop limit 1 and VPC CNI network policies, ECR and the AWS Load Balancer Controller via Pod Identity; GitHub Actions scans without credentials, then deploys over OIDC by digest with cosign signing, a least-privilege check and a smoke test through the ALB.
projects.unique_capability: Built and recorded on a real AWS account in 62 minutes: attacks refused (privileged pod, egress, IMDS), two real weaknesses found and fixed (lateral movement, dropped requests 3/280 to 401/401), verified teardown.

projects.name: Docker From Zero: a complete hands-on Docker learning lab
projects.simple_name: Learn Docker by running it, breaking it and fixing it
projects.summary: A free course you download and work through on your own computer. It starts with the very first Docker command and ends with a small three-part website you build, break on purpose, repair and check yourself. Every command in it has been run automatically, so what you read is what happens.
projects.problem: Most Docker tutorials only show the happy path. Beginners copy commands without knowing why they work, get stuck at the first real error, and many guides are already out of date with current Docker and database versions.
projects.benefit: Learners practise the real failures they will meet at work and learn to find the cause from evidence instead of guessing, with a guided path, labs, challenges, a final project, a two-part video and a printable study guide, using nothing but their own computer.
projects.tagline: From your first container to a full application, learned by doing, breaking and fixing.
projects.engineering_problem: Teaching material that drifts from reality: commands that no longer work, outputs that differ, and failures that are never shown.
projects.architecture: 23 concept lessons, 18 labs, a 12-chapter tutorial, 10 failure scenarios and 19 challenges around small example apps; the capstone runs nginx (non-root), a Python API (non-root, read-only, limits, health check) and PostgreSQL 18 on a named volume, split across frontend and backend networks, with the password as a secret file. A Markdown test runner executes every lesson on a fresh Docker engine, locally and in GitHub Actions, and writes the real output into the docs.
projects.unique_capability: Every one of the lesson commands is executed automatically and the shown outputs are real; the capstone verifies itself with 18 checks; images published for amd64 and arm64; image optimization measured at 1.75 GB -> 212 MB -> 108 MB.

projects.name: Kubernetes From Zero: installation and cluster setup, hands-on (kubeadm, Minikube, MicroK8s, Amazon EKS)
projects.simple_name: Set up Kubernetes four ways, then break it and fix it
projects.summary: A free course that takes someone who has never installed Kubernetes to four working clusters: one built by hand on two virtual machines, one on a laptop, one from a single package, and one in the cloud on AWS. Each one is checked the same way, broken on purpose, repaired, and removed again.
projects.problem: Most guides give you a list of commands to paste. When the cluster says "NotReady", a computer cannot join, or the cloud bill keeps running after a test, beginners have no idea why, and nobody showed them how to find out.
projects.benefit: Learners understand what every installation step does, practise eight realistic failures with a repeatable method, learn which setup fits which situation, and see a cloud cluster created and fully removed with proof that nothing was left behind.
projects.tagline: Install Kubernetes four ways, understand every step, and practise fixing what breaks.
projects.engineering_problem: Installation guides drift from reality and never show failures; cloud labs leave resources (and costs) behind.
projects.architecture: 13 concept lessons and four installation lessons written to one 15-point standard, 8 troubleshooting labs, 5 challenges, a capstone and a 12-chapter tutorial. A Markdown test runner executes every lesson on fresh Ubuntu VMs (LXD in GitHub Actions) and writes the real output back; the EKS lesson ran against AWS with eksctl, a read-only console walkthrough, and a verified teardown back to the starting inventory.
projects.unique_capability: Every lesson command runs automatically on real VMs; the EKS run measured 14.5 min to create and 11 min to delete, cost roughly $0.15-0.20, and left the region exactly as it was; an 18-chapter video in full and silent versions.

projects.name: Multi-Stack Applications on Kubernetes: from Docker Compose to Kubernetes (React, Node.js, Python, Go, Java, Laravel)
projects.simple_name: Seven different apps, one way to run them all
projects.summary: A free course with seven small applications, each written in a different programming language, that together make one online bookshop. You package each one, run them all together on your computer, and then move the whole shop onto Kubernetes, step by step, checking at every step that it really works.
projects.problem: Every language seems to need its own way of being deployed, so beginners copy settings they do not understand. Moving from a local setup to Kubernetes then feels like magic, and when something breaks nobody knows where to start looking.
projects.benefit: Learners see that the same few rules work for any language, understand why each Kubernetes building block exists, and practise twelve realistic failures until finding the cause becomes routine.
projects.tagline: Seven languages, one platform: from your laptop to Kubernetes, understood step by step.
projects.engineering_problem: Turning a multi-language Docker Compose setup into correct Kubernetes resources, with health checks, configuration, storage and safe updates, instead of a mechanical conversion.
projects.architecture: Seven services (React/nginx, Express, FastAPI, Go, Spring Boot, Laravel nginx+PHP-FPM, a JavaScript batch job) sharing one service contract and PostgreSQL. Docker Compose with health-aware dependencies and isolated networks; on kind: Deployments, a StatefulSet with a persistent volume, a migration Job, a CronJob, a two-container Pod, ConfigMaps, Secrets, probes, resources and a Traefik Ingress. Every lesson is tested Markdown run in CI.
projects.unique_capability: Every command in 7 app lessons, the Compose lesson, 15 Kubernetes lessons, 12 troubleshooting labs, 6 challenges and the capstone runs in CI; a deploy script builds the platform from nothing and a 22-check verification proves it, including an on-call scenario.

projects.name: Helm From Zero: Complete Hands-On Helm Learning Lab (charts, values, releases, rollbacks, troubleshooting)
projects.simple_name: One recipe for many copies of the same app
projects.summary: A free course that starts with an online shop set up three times (for testing, rehearsal and real customers) by copying the same long instruction files, and replaces the copies with one reusable recipe plus a short list of differences per environment. You install, update, undo and check the shop the way teams do every week, and practise twelve realistic mistakes.
projects.problem: Teams copy the same Kubernetes files for every environment. One change means editing every copy, forgotten copies drift apart, nothing records what was deployed, and passwords end up in the files.
projects.benefit: Learners can package an application once, run it in any number of environments from small settings files, see exactly what will change before an update, undo a bad update in one command, and investigate failed deployments with a repeatable method.
projects.tagline: From 1,374 lines of copied YAML to one chart, three short values files and a release history.
projects.engineering_problem: Replacing per-environment copies of Kubernetes manifests with a versioned chart, and operating it safely: reviewed upgrades, rollbacks, tests, secrets kept out of values and release history, and diagnosing Helm-specific failures.
projects.architecture: The multi-stack Bookshop (five services and PostgreSQL) as raw YAML for three environments, a lesson chart for its frontend, and a production-style chart: one range-driven template for all services, a local PostgreSQL subchart with a condition, a lookup-generated password kept across upgrades, a post-install/post-upgrade hook, Helm tests, an HPA and PodDisruptionBudgets for production. Charts are linted and validated with kubeconform for every values file and published to GHCR as OCI artifacts; every lesson is tested Markdown run on kind with Helm 4.3.
projects.unique_capability: Every command in 17 labs, the security and production-chart lessons, 12 troubleshooting scenarios (including immutable selectors, stuck pending-upgrade releases and Helm 4 server-side apply conflicts), 12 challenges and the 19-step capstone runs in CI.

projects.name: Git Practical Course: Git & GitHub From Beginner to Advanced (98 tested lessons, troubleshooting, capstone to Kubernetes)
projects.simple_name: A time machine for your files, and how to drive it
projects.summary: A free course on the tool every software team uses to keep the history of its work and combine everyone's changes. Ninety-eight short lessons, each with a practice folder, show a step, make a typical mistake on purpose and repair it, so that learners stay calm when something goes wrong at work. It ends with a project that publishes and deploys a small website automatically.
projects.problem: People learn Git as a list of commands, then lose time and work on what really happens in teams: conflicts, rejected pushes, lost commits, rewritten history, secrets in the history, team rules.
projects.benefit: Learners can work safely in a shared repository, recover from almost any mistake, review and merge changes through pull requests, protect important branches, and release and deploy from Git tags.
projects.tagline: 98 lessons, 18 troubleshooting labs, 6 projects and a capstone released to Kubernetes; every command tested.
projects.engineering_problem: Teaching Git through realistic failures, with every command and output verified automatically, including the GitHub workflows (pull requests, protection, releases, Actions).
projects.architecture: Ninety-eight Markdown lessons that are also tests: a runner executes every Bash block in a sandbox (temporary home, ssh shim, own kubeconfig, a copy of the course without .git) and writes the real outputs back. Labs start from deterministic histories, so every learner sees the same commit IDs. CI runs all 1,308 blocks with the latest Git in four parallel groups; 153 blocks run against GitHub. A DevOps template repository (app, Dockerfile, Helm chart, CI) drives module 21, project 6 (tag-driven deploys to kind) and the capstone, whose release workflow pushes to GHCR and deploys with Helm to a kind cluster.
projects.unique_capability: Every lesson includes a deliberate mistake and its fix; 18 troubleshooting labs; self-check graders for the projects, the capstone and the final exam; a 23-video series generated from the lessons with two narrator voices and real outputs.

projects.name: Docker Practical Course: Docker From Beginner to Advanced (116 tested lessons, 25 troubleshooting problems, hardened capstone)
projects.simple_name: Shipping containers for software, and what to do when one breaks
projects.summary: A free course on packaging applications so they run the same everywhere. A hundred and sixteen short lessons each run something, look inside it, break it on purpose and repair it, so that learners can read the error and fix it when it happens at work. It ends with a small online shop system built, secured, checked and shipped the way teams do it.
projects.problem: People learn Docker as a few commands, then lose time on what goes wrong in real use: ports, networks and names, permissions, lost data, memory kills, unhealthy services, slow builds and leaked secrets.
projects.benefit: Learners can containerize applications in five languages, connect and persist them, secure and measure them, troubleshoot the common failures from symptom to prevention, and ship images through a registry and CI to Kubernetes.
projects.tagline: 116 lessons, 25 troubleshooting problems, 8 projects and a hardened capstone stack; every command tested.
projects.engineering_problem: Teaching Docker through realistic failures, with every command and output verified automatically on both Docker Desktop and a Linux engine.
projects.architecture: A hundred and sixteen Markdown lessons that are also tests: a runner executes every Bash block in a sandbox (temporary home, separate Docker CLI configuration and kubeconfig, a copy of the course), starts every lesson from an empty engine and writes the real outputs back. CI runs all 1,777 blocks on Docker Engine 29 in four parallel groups, with a pull-through mirror, the containerd image store, QEMU and kind. The capstone (Nginx proxy, frontend, Go API, PostgreSQL) uses multi-stage builds, an internal network, a secret file, healthchecks, limits, read-only file systems and dropped capabilities; its workflow pushes the images to GHCR.
projects.unique_capability: Every lesson includes a deliberate failure and its fix; 25 troubleshooting problems; a graded final exam; lessons corrected where Linux and Docker Desktop behave differently; a 21-video series generated from the lessons with two narrator voices and real outputs.
